label: Set
statement: A set is a mathematical collection of objects, called elements.
formal_statement: Set theory treats membership $x\in A$ as the primitive relation between an object $x$ and a set $A$.
definition: A collection considered as a single mathematical object.
intuition: The raw substrate of topology: a space starts as a set before any open sets are chosen.
full_text: Set | A set is a mathematical collection of objects, called elements. | A collection considered as a single mathematical object. | The raw substrate of topology: a space starts as a set before any open sets are chosen.

label: Function
statement: A function $f:X\to Y$ assigns each element of its domain $X$ exactly one element of its codomain $Y$.
formal_statement: $f\subseteq X\times Y$ and for every $x\in X$ there exists a unique $y\in Y$ with $(x,y)\in f$.
definition: A single-valued, total relation from a domain to a codomain.
intuition: A rule with no ambiguity: every input has exactly one output.
full_text: Function | A function $f:X\to Y$ assigns each element of its domain $X$ exactly one element of its codomain $Y$. | A single-valued, total relation from a domain to a codomain. | A rule with no ambiguity: every input has exactly one output.

label: Inverse Image
statement: The inverse image of a set $B$ under a function $f:X\to Y$ is the set of all elements in $X$ that map into $B$.
definition: The preimage of a set under a function.
intuition: The set of inputs that land in a given set under the function.
full_text: Inverse Image | The inverse image of a set $B$ under a function $f:X\to Y$ is the set of all elements in $X$ that map into $B$. | The preimage of a set under a function. | The set of inputs that land in a given set under the function.

label: Inverse of a Function
statement: The inverse relation of a function $f:X\to Y$ reverses the ordered pairs of $f$. It is a function $Y\to X$ exactly when $f$ is bijective.
definition: The relation obtained by swapping the inputs and outputs of a function.
intuition: This records the backward relation. Extra hypotheses such as bijectivity are needed before it becomes a genuine inverse function.
full_text: Inverse of a Function | The inverse relation of a function $f:X\to Y$ reverses the ordered pairs of $f$. It is a function $Y\to X$ exactly when $f$ is bijective. | The relation obtained by swapping the inputs and outputs of a function. | This records the backward relation. Extra hypotheses such as bijectivity are needed before it becomes a genuine inverse function.

label: Image of a Function
statement: The image of a function $f:X\to Y$ is the set of all outputs of $f$.
definition: The set of outputs of a function.
intuition: The set of values that the function actually takes on.
full_text: Image of a Function | The image of a function $f:X\to Y$ is the set of all outputs of $f$. | The set of outputs of a function. | The set of values that the function actually takes on.

label: Preimage of a Function
statement: The preimage relation of a function $f:X\to Y$ records which inputs map to each output.
formal_statement: $f^{-1}=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in f\}\subseteq Y\times X$.
definition: The inverse relation associated to a function.
intuition: This relation is the pointwise data behind set preimages $f^{-1}(B)$, but it need not itself be single-valued.
full_text: Preimage of a Function | The preimage relation of a function $f:X\to Y$ records which inputs map to each output. | The inverse relation associated to a function. | This relation is the pointwise data behind set preimages $f^{-1}(B)$, but it need not itself be single-valued.

label: Inverse of a Function
statement: The inverse of a function $f:X\to Y$ is the relation that reverses the direction of $f$.
definition: The relation obtained by swapping the inputs and outputs of a function.
intuition: The function that goes backwards: it takes outputs of $f$ and gives you back the inputs.
full_text: Inverse of a Function | The inverse of a function $f:X\to Y$ is the relation that reverses the direction of $f$. | The relation obtained by swapping the inputs and outputs of a function. | The function that goes backwards: it takes outputs of $f$ and gives you back the inputs.

label: Restriction of a Function
statement: The restriction of a function $f:X\to Y$ to a subset $A\subseteq X$ is the function obtained by limiting the domain of $f$ to $A$.
formal_statement: $f|_A : A \to Y$ defined by $f|_A(a) = f(a)$ for all $a\in A$.
definition: The function obtained by limiting the domain of a function to a subset.
intuition: The same rule as the original function, but only applied to a smaller set of inputs.
full_text: Restriction of a Function | The restriction of a function $f:X\to Y$ to a subset $A\subseteq X$ is the function obtained by limiting the domain of $f$ to $A$. | The function obtained by limiting the domain of a function to a subset. | The same rule as the original function, but only applied to a smaller set of inputs.

label: Axiom of Choice
statement: Every indexed family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
formal_statement: If $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ and $A_i\ne\varnothing$ for all $i$, then there exists $c:I\to\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i$ such that $c(i)\in A_i$ for all $i$.
intuition: You may choose one element from each set in a family, even when there is no explicit rule for making the choices.
full_text: Axiom of Choice | Every indexed family of nonempty sets has a choice function. | You may choose one element from each set in a family, even when there is no explicit rule for making the choices.

label: Topological Space
statement: A \textbf{topological space} is a pair $(X,\mathcal{T})$ where $X$ is a set and $\mathcal{T}$ is a topology on $X$. The topology is the second component of the pair, and its elements are the open sets of the space.
formal_statement: A topological space is a pair $(X,\mathcal{T})$ such that $X$ is a set and $\mathcal{T}\in\operatorname{Top}(X)$.
definition: A pair $(X,\mathcal{T})$ consisting of a set and a topology on it.
intuition: A topological space packages the underlying set together with its chosen topology.
gloss: The central object of topology: a set together with a choice of which subsets count as open.

The topology is the second component of the pair, and its elements are the open sets of the space. | A pair $(X,\mathcal{T})$ consisting of a set and a topology on it. | A topological space packages the underlying set together with its chosen topology. | The central object of topology: a set together with a choice of which subsets count as open.

label: Pseudometric Space
statement: A set with a pseudometric, allowing distinct points at distance zero.
definition: A set with a pseudometric, allowing distinct points at distance zero.

label: Metric Space
statement: A \textbf{metric space} $(X,d)$ is a non-empty set $X$ with a map $d\colon X\times X\to\mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x,y,z\in X$: $$\begin{aligned} \textbf{(M1)}\quad d(x,y) &\ge 0,\ \text{and}\ d(x,y)=0\Leftrightarrow x=y \\ \textbf{(M2)}\quad d(x,y) &= d(y,x) \\ \textbf{(M3)}\quad d(x,z) &\le d(x,y)+d(y,z). \end{aligned}$$
formal_statement: Let $(M,d)$ with $d:M\times M\to[0,\infty)$, then $$\begin{align} d(x,y) &= 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad x=y \\ d(x,y) &= d(y,x) \\ d(x,z) &\le d(x,y)+d(y,z) \end{align}$$
definition: A set with a distance function satisfying positivity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality.
intuition: Topology with numerical distance still visible.
gloss: A set equipped with a notion of distance. The three axioms say distance is non-negative (and zero only between identical points), symmetric, and obeys the triangle inequality.

The three axioms say distance is non-negative (and zero only between identical points), symmetric, and obeys the triangle inequality.

label: Subspace
statement: A subset equipped with the induced subspace topology.
definition: A subset equipped with the induced subspace topology.
full_text: Subspace | A subset equipped with the induced subspace topology. | A subset equipped with the induced subspace topology.

label: Product Space
statement: A Cartesian product equipped with the product topology.
definition: A Cartesian product equipped with the product topology.
full_text: Product Space | A Cartesian product equipped with the product topology. | A Cartesian product equipped with the product topology.

label: Quotient Space
statement: For a surjection $\pi\colon X\to A$ from a space $X$, the \textbf{quotient topology} on $A$ is $\{U\subseteq A\mid \pi^{-1}(U)\ \text{open in}\ X\}$. Then $\pi$ is a \textbf{quotient map} and $A$ the \textbf{quotient space}.
definition: A set of equivalence classes equipped with the quotient topology.
gloss: Glue points of $X$ together (via $\pi$) and declare a set in $A$ open exactly when its preimage is open. It is the finest topology making $\pi$ continuous.
full_text: Quotient Space | For a surjection $\pi\colon X\to A$ from a space $X$, the \textbf{quotient topology} on $A$ is $\{U\subseteq A\mid \pi^{-1}(U)\ \text{open in}\ X\}$. Then $\pi$ is a \textbf{quotient map} and $A$ the \textbf{quotient space}. | A set of equivalence classes equipped with the quotient topology. | Glue points of $X$ together (via $\pi$) and declare a set in $A$ open exactly when its preimage is open. It is the finest topology making $\pi$ continuous.

label: Compact Space
statement: $X$ is \textbf{compact} if every open cover of $X$ has a finite subcover.
definition: A topological space satisfying compactness.
gloss: No matter how you cover $X$ with open sets, finitely many already suffice. A powerful finiteness condition standing in for “closed and bounded.”
full_text: Compact Space | $X$ is \textbf{compact} if every open cover of $X$ has a finite subcover. | A topological space satisfying compactness. | No matter how you cover $X$ with open sets, finitely many already suffice. A powerful finiteness condition standing in for “closed and bounded.”

label: Connected Space
statement: A \textbf{separation} of $X$ is a pair of disjoint non-empty open sets $U,V$ with $U\cup V=X$. $X$ is \textbf{connected} if it has no separation; otherwise \textbf{disconnected}.
definition: A topological space satisfying connectedness.
gloss: Connected means the space cannot be split into two non-trivial open pieces — equivalently, its only clopen subsets are $\varnothing$ and $X$.
full_text: Connected Space | A \textbf{separation} of $X$ is a pair of disjoint non-empty open sets $U,V$ with $U\cup V=X$. $X$ is \textbf{connected} if it has no separation; otherwise \textbf{disconnected}. | A topological space satisfying connectedness. | Connected means the space cannot be split into two non-trivial open pieces — equivalently, its only clopen subsets are $\varnothing$ and $X$.

label: Path-Connected Space
statement: A \textbf{path} from $x$ to $y$ is a continuous map $f\colon[a,b]\to X$ with $f(a)=x$, $f(b)=y$. $X$ is \textbf{path-connected} if any two points are joined by a path.
definition: A topological space satisfying path connectedness.
gloss: You can walk continuously between any two points. A stronger, more geometric cousin of connectedness.
full_text: Path-Connected Space | A \textbf{path} from $x$ to $y$ is a continuous map $f\colon[a,b]\to X$ with $f(a)=x$, $f(b)=y$. $X$ is \textbf{path-connected} if any two points are joined by a path. | A topological space satisfying path connectedness. | You can walk continuously between any two points. A stronger, more geometric cousin of connectedness.

label: Hausdorff Space
statement: $X$ is \textbf{Hausdorff} ($T_2$) if for all distinct $x,y\in X$ there are disjoint open sets $U\ni x$ and $V\ni y$.
definition: A topological space satisfying the Hausdorff property.
gloss: Distinct points can be “housed” in disjoint neighborhoods. This separation guarantees limits are unique and compact sets are closed.
full_text: Hausdorff Space | $X$ is \textbf{Hausdorff} ($T_2$) if for all distinct $x,y\in X$ there are disjoint open sets $U\ni x$ and $V\ni y$. | A topological space satisfying the Hausdorff property. | Distinct points can be “housed” in disjoint neighborhoods. This separation guarantees limits are unique and compact sets are closed.

label: Regular Space
statement: Under the atlas default convention, a regular space is a T1 topological space in which points and disjoint closed sets can be separated by disjoint open neighborhoods.
formal_statement: $$(X,\tau)\text{ regular}\Longleftrightarrow [\forall x\in X,\ \{x\}\text{ is closed}]\ \land\ \forall x\in X\ \forall F\subseteq X,\ (F\text{ closed}\land x\notin F)\Rightarrow \exists U,V\in\tau\ (x\in U,\ F\subseteq V,\ U\cap V=\varnothing).$$
definition: Using the atlas default T1 convention, a topological space is regular if singletons are closed and every point can be separated from every closed set not containing it by disjoint open sets.
intuition: Regularity says a point and a closed obstacle can be pulled apart topologically.
full_text: Regular Space | Under the atlas default convention, a regular space is a T1 topological space in which points and disjoint closed sets can be separated by disjoint open neighborhoods. | Using the atlas default T1 convention, a topological space is regular if singletons are closed and every point can be separated from every closed set not containing it by disjoint open sets. | Regularity says a point and a closed obstacle can be pulled apart topologically.

label: Normal Space
statement: Under the atlas default convention, a normal space is a T1 topological space in which disjoint closed sets can be separated by disjoint open neighborhoods.
formal_statement: $$(X,\tau)\text{ normal}\Longleftrightarrow [\forall x\in X,\ \{x\}\text{ is closed}]\ \land\ \forall F,G\subseteq X,\ (F,G\text{ closed}\land F\cap G=\varnothing)\Rightarrow \exists U,V\in\tau\ (F\subseteq U,\ G\subseteq V,\ U\cap V=\varnothing).$$
definition: Using the atlas default T1 convention, a topological space is normal if singletons are closed and every pair of disjoint closed subsets can be separated by disjoint open neighborhoods.
intuition: Normality is closed-set separation: two closed pieces can be insulated from one another by open regions.
full_text: Normal Space | Under the atlas default convention, a normal space is a T1 topological space in which disjoint closed sets can be separated by disjoint open neighborhoods. | Using the atlas default T1 convention, a topological space is normal if singletons are closed and every pair of disjoint closed subsets can be separated by disjoint open neighborhoods. | Normality is closed-set separation: two closed pieces can be insulated from one another by open regions.

label: Locally Compact Space
statement: $X$ is \textbf{locally compact} if every point has a compact neighborhood.
formal_statement: $$X\text{ locally compact}\Longleftrightarrow \forall x\in X\ \exists N\subseteq X\ \big(N\in\mathcal N_X(x)\ \land\ N\text{ is compact in the subspace topology}\big).$$
definition: A topological space is locally compact if every point has a neighborhood that is compact as a subspace. Under Hausdorff-type assumptions this is often expressed using open neighborhoods with compact closure.
intuition: A space that is compact in the small — the natural setting for one-point compactification and for much of analysis.
gloss: Each point has a compact neighborhood, so the space looks compact near any given point.
full_text: Locally Compact Space | $X$ is \textbf{locally compact} if every point has a compact neighborhood. | A topological space is locally compact if every point has a neighborhood that is compact as a subspace. Under Hausdorff-type assumptions this is often expressed using open neighborhoods with compact closure. | A space that is compact in the small — the natural setting for one-point compactification and for much of analysis. | Each point has a compact neighborhood, so the space looks compact near any given point.

label: Second-Countable Space
statement: A topological space with a countable basis.
definition: A topological space with a countable basis.
full_text: Second-Countable Space | A topological space with a countable basis. | A topological space with a countable basis.

label: Manifold
statement: Under the atlas default convention, an $n$-manifold is a Hausdorff, second-countable topological space locally homeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$.
formal_statement: $$X\text{ is an }n\text{-manifold}\Longleftrightarrow X\text{ is Hausdorff and second-countable, and }\forall x\in X\ \exists U\ni x\ \exists V\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ open with }U\cong V.$$
definition: A topological manifold without boundary is a Hausdorff, second-countable topological space such that every point has an open neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$.
intuition: A manifold is a space that may be globally curved or glued, but locally looks like ordinary Euclidean space.

label: Compact Hausdorff Space
statement: A space that is both compact and Hausdorff.
definition: A space that is both compact and Hausdorff.
intuition: The “best-behaved” compact spaces: points are separated, compact subsets are closed, and continuous bijections out of them are homeomorphisms.
gloss: Compactness plus the Hausdorff separation axiom — the combination behind many rigidity theorems.

label: Topology
statement: A topology on a set $X$ is a collection $\tau\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ containing $\varnothing$ and $X$ and closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections.
formal_statement: $$ \begin{aligned} &\tau \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X), \qquad \varnothing, X \in \tau, \\ &\{U_i\}_{i \in I} \subseteq \tau \quad \Rightarrow \quad \bigcup_{i \in I} U_i \in \tau, \\ &U_1,\ldots,U_n \in \tau \quad \Rightarrow \quad \bigcap_{k=1}^{n} U_k \in \tau. \end{aligned} $$
definition: Given a set $X$, a topology $\tau$ on $X$ is a specified collection of subsets of $X$, called open sets, satisfying the topology axioms.
intuition: A topology is the open-set structure placed on a set. It is the collection $\tau$ itself, not the resulting space $(X,\tau)$.
full_text: Topology | A topology on a set $X$ is a collection $\tau\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ containing $\varnothing$ and $X$ and closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections. | Given a set $X$, a topology $\tau$ on $X$ is a specified collection of subsets of $X$, called open sets, satisfying the topology axioms. | A topology is the open-set structure placed on a set. It is the collection $\tau$ itself, not the resulting space $(X,\tau)$.

label: Open Set
statement: In a topological space $(X, \mathcal{T})$, a subset $U$ of $X$ is open exactly when $U$ belongs to $\mathcal{T}$.
formal_statement: $$U\subseteq X \text{ is open in }(X,\mathcal{T})\Longleftrightarrow U\in\mathcal{T}.$$
definition: An open set of a topological space (X, τ) is a subset U⊆X that is an element of the topology τ.
intuition: Open sets are the primitive observable neighborhoods of the space; all topological notions are expressed in terms of them.
full_text: Open Set | In a topological space $(X, \mathcal{T})$, a subset $U$ of $X$ is open exactly when $U$ belongs to $\mathcal{T}$. | An open set of a topological space (X, τ) is a subset U⊆X that is an element of the topology τ. | Open sets are the primitive observable neighborhoods of the space; all topological notions are expressed in terms of them.

label: Closed Set
statement: A subset C of a topological space X is closed exactly when its complement in X is open.
formal_statement: $$C\subseteq X \text{ is closed in }(X,\tau)\Longleftrightarrow X\setminus C\in\tau.$$
definition: For a topological space (X, τ), a subset C⊆X is closed in X if its complement X\C is open in X.
intuition: Closed sets are the subsets whose outside is topologically open; they contain their limit behavior as far as the topology detects it.
gloss: Closed = complement is open. Closed sets satisfy the dual axioms: arbitrary intersections and finite unions of closed sets are closed (Thm. 3.28).
full_text: Closed Set | A subset C of a topological space X is closed exactly when its complement in X is open. | For a topological space (X, τ), a subset C⊆X is closed in X if its complement X\C is open in X. | Closed sets are the subsets whose outside is topologically open; they contain their limit behavior as far as the topology detects it. | Closed = complement is open. Closed sets satisfy the dual axioms: arbitrary intersections and finite unions of closed sets are closed (Thm. 3.28).

label: Neighborhood
statement: A subset N of a topological space X is a neighborhood of x if it contains an open set that contains x.
formal_statement: $$N\in\mathcal N_X(x)\Longleftrightarrow \exists U\in\mathcal T\ \text{such that}\ x\in U\subseteq N.$$
definition: In a topological space $(X,\mathcal T)$, a subset $N\subseteq X$ is a neighborhood of $x\in X$ if there exists an open set $U\in\mathcal T$ such that $x\in U\subseteq N$.
intuition: A neighborhood is any set large enough to contain a genuinely open region around the point; it does not have to be open itself under the broad convention.
gloss: Broad convention: a neighborhood may be non-open, as long as it contains an open set around the point. When the set itself is open, call it an open neighborhood.

When the set itself is open, call it an open neighborhood.

label: Basis for a Topology
statement: A basis for an existing topology is a collection of open sets such that every open set is a union of basis elements.
formal_statement: $$\mathcal B\subseteq\tau\text{ is a basis for }(X,\tau)\Longleftrightarrow \forall U\in\tau\ \forall x\in U\ \exists B\in\mathcal B\ (x\in B\subseteq U).$$
definition: For a topological space (X, τ), a basis is a collection B of open subsets of X such that for every open set U and every point x∈U, there is B∈B with x∈B⊆U. Equivalently, every open set is a union of basis elements.
intuition: A basis gives small reusable open pieces from which all open sets are assembled by unions.
gloss: A small kit of sets from which all open sets are built as unions. Open $=$ union of basis elements (Thm. 4.10).

Equivalently, every open set is a union of basis elements. | A basis gives small reusable open pieces from which all open sets are assembled by unions. | A small kit of sets from which all open sets are built as unions. Open $=$ union of basis elements (Thm. 4.10).

label: Subbasis
statement: A subbasis is a collection of subsets whose finite intersections form a basis for the topology it generates.
formal_statement: $$\tau(\mathcal S)=\left\{\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\bigcap_{k=1}^{n_\lambda}S_{\lambda,k}:S_{\lambda,k}\in\mathcal S,\ n_\lambda<\infty\right\}.$$
definition: A subbasis is a collection of subsets whose finite intersections form a basis for the topology generated by it; arbitrary unions of those finite intersections are the open sets.
intuition: A subbasis specifies even simpler open constraints; finite intersections make basic opens, and arbitrary unions make all opens.
gloss: An even smaller seed: take finite intersections to get a basis, then unions to get the topology. Open sets are unions of finite intersections of subbasis elements.

Open sets are unions of finite intersections of subbasis elements.

label: Closure
statement: The closure of A in X is the smallest closed subset of X containing A.
formal_statement: $$\operatorname{cl}_X(A)=\overline A=\bigcap\{F\subseteq X: A\subseteq F\ \text{and}\ F \text{ is closed in }X\}.$$
definition: For A⊆X, the closure cl_X(A) is the intersection of all closed subsets of X that contain A; equivalently, it is the least closed subset of X containing A.
intuition: The closure adds all points that cannot be separated from A by open neighborhoods.
gloss: The closure adds exactly the points $A$ “almost reaches.” If $A$ is already closed then $\overline{A}=A$.
full_text: Closure | The closure of A in X is the smallest closed subset of X containing A. | For A⊆X, the closure cl_X(A) is the intersection of all closed subsets of X that contain A; equivalently, it is the least closed subset of X containing A. | The closure adds all points that cannot be separated from A by open neighborhoods. | The closure adds exactly the points $A$ “almost reaches.” If $A$ is already closed then $\overline{A}=A$.

label: Interior
statement: For a subset A of a topological space X, the interior of A is the largest open subset of X contained in A.
formal_statement: $$\operatorname{int}_X(A)=A^\circ=\bigcup\{U\in\tau_X:U\subseteq A\}.$$
definition: Let $(X,\tau_X)$ be a topological space and let $A\subseteq X$. The interior of $A$ in $X$, denoted $\operatorname{int}_X(A)$ or $A^\circ$, is the union of all open subsets of $X$ contained in $A$. Equivalently, it is the largest open subset of $X$ contained in $A$.
intuition: The interior keeps exactly the points of $A$ that have room around them: a point $x$ lies in $\operatorname{int}_X(A)$ precisely when some open neighborhood of $x$ is contained entirely in $A$. Boundary points fail this test because every open neighborhood around them leaks outside $A$.
gloss: Dual to closure: closure expands $A$ by adding unavoidable nearby points, while interior trims $A$ down to the points it surrounds with open room. Always $$\operatorname{int}_X(A)\subseteq A\subseteq\overline{A}.$$

label: Boundary
statement: The boundary of A is the part of the closure of A outside the interior of A.
formal_statement: $$\partial_X A=\overline A\setminus A^\circ=\overline A\cap\overline{X\setminus A}.$$
definition: For A⊆X, the boundary ∂_X A is cl_X(A)\int_X(A). Equivalently, it is the set of points whose every neighborhood meets both A and X\A.
intuition: Boundary points are exactly the points where the topology cannot see a whole neighborhood lying entirely inside A or entirely outside A.

label: Dense Subset
statement: A subset A of X is dense in X exactly when its closure is all of X.
formal_statement: $$A\subseteq X \text{ is dense in }X\Longleftrightarrow \overline A=X\Longleftrightarrow \forall\,\varnothing\ne U\in\tau,\ U\cap A\ne\varnothing.$$
definition: For a topological space X, a subset A⊆X is dense in X if cl_X(A)=X. Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of X intersects A.
intuition: A dense subset is topologically unavoidable: every nonempty open region of the space contains a point of it.
gloss: A dense set is everywhere — its closure fills the whole space, so it meets every open set.

label: Continuity
statement: A map between topological spaces is continuous exactly when inverse images of open sets are open.
formal_statement: $$f:(X,\tau_X)\to(Y,\tau_Y)\text{ is continuous}\Longleftrightarrow \forall V\in\tau_Y,\ f^{-1}(V)\in\tau_X.$$
definition: Given topological spaces (X, τ_X) and (Y, τ_Y), a function f:X→Y is continuous if the preimage of every open subset of Y is open in X.
intuition: Continuity means that topological tests made by open sets in the codomain pull back to valid open tests in the domain.
gloss: Continuity means that open regions in the target pull back to open regions in the domain. This is the full topological definition: it uses only the open-set structure, not distances, balls, or a metric.

label: Homeomorphism
statement: A homeomorphism is a bijective continuous map whose inverse is also continuous.
formal_statement: $$f:X\to Y\text{ is a homeomorphism}\Longleftrightarrow f\text{ is bijective},\ f\text{ is continuous},\ \text{and }f^{-1}:Y\to X\text{ is continuous}.$$
definition: For topological spaces X and Y, a homeomorphism is a bijection f:X→Y such that both f and its inverse f^{-1}:Y→X are continuous. If such a map exists, X and Y are homeomorphic.
intuition: A homeomorphism is an isomorphism of topological spaces: it preserves and reflects exactly the open-set structure.
gloss: The notion of sameness in topology: two spaces are homeomorphic when one can be transformed into the other by a reversible continuous deformation. their open-set structures correspond perfectly in both directions.

label: Convergence
statement: A net converges to x when it is eventually contained in every neighborhood of x.
formal_statement: $$(x_i)_{i\in I}\to x\Longleftrightarrow \forall N\in\mathcal N_X(x)\ \exists i_0\in I\ \forall i\ge i_0,\ x_i\in N.$$
definition: In a topological space X, a net (x_i) indexed by a directed set I converges to x∈X if for every neighborhood N of x, the net is eventually in N. For sequences, I=ℕ with its usual order.
intuition: Convergence means that every topological test neighborhood of the proposed limit eventually contains all later terms.

For sequences, I=ℕ with its usual order. | Convergence means that every topological test neighborhood of the proposed limit eventually contains all later terms.

label: Compactness
statement: A topological space is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover.
formal_statement: $$(X,\mathcal T)\text{ compact}\Longleftrightarrow \forall\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal T,\ \left(X\subseteq\bigcup_{U\in\mathcal U}U\Rightarrow \exists U_1,\ldots,U_n\in\mathcal U\text{ such that }X\subseteq\bigcup_{k=1}^{n}U_k\right).$$
definition: Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space. A collection $\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal T$ is an open cover of $X$ if $X=\bigcup_{U\in\mathcal U}U$. The space $(X,\mathcal T)$ is compact if every open cover $\mathcal U$ of $X$ contains a finite subcover.
intuition: Compactness says that whenever the whole space is described by possibly infinitely many open pieces, finitely many of those pieces already describe the whole space. It is a topological finiteness condition, not a size condition.
gloss: No matter how you cover $X$ with open sets, finitely many already suffice. A topological stand-in for “finite” — not about size, but about no escaping to infinity.
notation: $$\begin{aligned} \mathcal U&=\text{an open cover of }X,\\ \mathcal U_0&=\{U_1,\dots,U_n\}\subseteq\mathcal U=\text{a finite subcover},\\ X&=U_1\cup\cdots\cup U_n. \end{aligned}$$

label: Finite Intersection Property Characterization
statement: A space is compact exactly when every closed family with the finite intersection property has nonempty total intersection.
formal_statement: $$X\text{ compact}\Longleftrightarrow \forall\mathcal F\subseteq\{F\subseteq X:F\text{ closed}\},\ \left[\left(\forall F_1,\ldots,F_n\in\mathcal F,\ \bigcap_{k=1}^{n}F_k\ne\varnothing\right)\Rightarrow \bigcap_{F\in\mathcal F}F\ne\varnothing\right].$$
definition: The finite intersection property characterization says that compactness is equivalent to the following closed-set condition: whenever a family of closed subsets has nonempty intersection for every finite subfamily, the whole family has nonempty intersection.
intuition: This is the closed-set dual of the open-cover definition: failure of a finite subcover corresponds to finite intersections remaining nonempty.
gloss: The closed-set dual of compactness: shrinking closed sets that never disjointly vanish in finite batches must share a common point.

label: Sequential Compactness
statement: A topological space is sequentially compact when every sequence has a convergent subsequence whose limit lies in the space.
formal_statement: $$X\text{ sequentially compact}\Longleftrightarrow \forall (x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\in X^{\mathbb N},\ \exists n_1<n_2<\cdots,\ \exists x\in X\text{ such that }x_{n_k}\to x.$$
definition: A topological space X is sequentially compact if every sequence in X has a subsequence that converges to a point of X.
intuition: Sequential compactness is a sequence-based finiteness property; in general topology it is not equivalent to open-cover compactness without additional hypotheses.
gloss: Every sequence has a subsequence settling down to a point of the space. Equivalent to compactness for metric spaces, but not in general.

label: Connectedness
statement: A topological space is connected when it cannot be separated into two disjoint nonempty open subsets.
formal_statement: $$X\text{ connected}\Longleftrightarrow \nexists U,V\in\tau\ \text{with }U,V\ne\varnothing,\ U\cap V=\varnothing,\ \text{and }X=U\cup V.$$
definition: A topological space X is connected if there do not exist disjoint nonempty open subsets U,V⊆X whose union is X. Equivalently, the only subsets of X that are both open and closed are ∅ and X.
intuition: Connectedness means the topology does not split the whole space into two separated open pieces.

Equivalently, the only subsets of X that are both open and closed are ∅ and X. | Connectedness means the topology does not split the whole space into two separated open pieces.

label: Path-Connectedness
statement: A topological space is path connected when every two points can be joined by a continuous path.
formal_statement: $$X\text{ path connected}\Longleftrightarrow \forall x,y\in X,\ \exists \gamma:[0,1]\to X\text{ continuous with }\gamma(0)=x,\ \gamma(1)=y.$$
definition: A topological space X is path connected if for every pair of points x,y∈X there is a continuous map γ:[0,1]→X from the unit interval to X with γ(0)=x and γ(1)=y.
intuition: Path connectedness is connectedness witnessed by actual continuous paths between points; it is stronger than connectedness in general.

label: Hausdorff Property
statement: A topological space is Hausdorff if any two distinct points have disjoint open neighborhoods.
formal_statement: $$(X,\mathcal T)\text{ is Hausdorff}\Longleftrightarrow \forall x,y\in X,\ x\ne y\Rightarrow \exists U,V\in\mathcal T\ \text{such that }x\in U,\ y\in V,\ U\cap V=\varnothing.$$
definition: A topological space X is Hausdorff, or T2, if for every pair of distinct points x,y∈X there are disjoint open sets U and V with x∈U and y∈V.
intuition: Hausdorffness says distinct points can be topologically pulled apart by nonoverlapping open regions.

label: Regularity
statement: Under the common T1 convention, a space is regular if points and disjoint closed sets can be separated by disjoint open neighborhoods.
formal_statement: $$(X,\tau)\text{ regular}\Longleftrightarrow [\forall x\in X,\ \{x\}\text{ is closed}]\ \land\ \forall x\in X\ \forall F\subseteq X,\ (F\text{ closed}\land x\notin F)\Rightarrow \exists U,V\in\tau\ (x\in U,\ F\subseteq V,\ U\cap V=\varnothing).$$
definition: Using the common T1 convention, a topological space X is regular if singletons are closed and, whenever F is closed and x∉F, there are disjoint open sets U,V with x∈U and F⊆V.
intuition: Regularity separates a point from a closed obstacle by disjoint open regions.

label: Normality
statement: Under the common T1 convention, a space is normal if disjoint closed sets can be separated by disjoint open neighborhoods.
formal_statement: $$(X,\tau)\text{ normal}\Longleftrightarrow [\forall x\in X,\ \{x\}\text{ is closed}]\ \land\ \forall F,G\subseteq X,\ (F,G\text{ closed}\land F\cap G=\varnothing)\Rightarrow \exists U,V\in\tau\ (F\subseteq U,\ G\subseteq V,\ U\cap V=\varnothing).$$
definition: Using the common T1 convention, a topological space X is normal if singletons are closed and every pair of disjoint closed subsets F,G⊆X has disjoint open neighborhoods U,V with F⊆U and G⊆V.
intuition: Normality is a strong separation property for closed sets, not just for individual points.

label: Countability Axioms
statement: Countability axioms require bases or local neighborhood bases to be countable.
formal_statement: $$\text{First countable: }\forall x\in X\,\exists\mathcal B_x\subseteq\mathcal N_X(x)\ (|\mathcal B_x|\le\aleph_0\ \text{and }\mathcal B_x\text{ is local at }x);\quad \text{Second countable: }\exists\mathcal B\text{ basis for }\tau,\ |\mathcal B|\le\aleph_0.$$
definition: Countability axioms are topological size restrictions on local or global bases, most commonly first countability and second countability.
intuition: They say that the topology can be probed using only countably many local or global open pieces.
full_text: Countability Axioms | Countability axioms require bases or local neighborhood bases to be countable. | Countability axioms are topological size restrictions on local or global bases, most commonly first countability and second countability. | They say that the topology can be probed using only countably many local or global open pieces.

label: First Countability
statement: A space is first countable if each point has a countable neighborhood basis.
formal_statement: $$X\text{ first countable}\Longleftrightarrow \forall x\in X\ \exists\mathcal B_x\subseteq\mathcal N_X(x)\ \left(|\mathcal B_x|\le\aleph_0\ \land\ \forall N\in\mathcal N_X(x)\ \exists B\in\mathcal B_x,\ x\in B\subseteq N\right).$$
definition: A topological space X is first countable if for every point x∈X there is a countable collection of neighborhoods of x such that every neighborhood of x contains one of them.
intuition: First countability gives each point a countable local scale of neighborhoods, making sequences more informative.

label: Second Countability
statement: A space is second countable if its topology has a countable basis.
formal_statement: $$X\text{ second countable}\Longleftrightarrow \exists\mathcal B\subseteq\tau\ \left(\mathcal B\text{ is a basis for }\tau\ \land\ |\mathcal B|\le\aleph_0\right).$$
definition: A topological space (X, τ) is second countable if there exists a countable basis for τ.
intuition: Second countability gives a countable global vocabulary for all open sets.

label: Local Compactness
statement: A space is locally compact if every point has a compact neighborhood.
formal_statement: $$X\text{ locally compact}\Longleftrightarrow \forall x\in X\ \exists N\in\mathcal N_X(x)\ \text{such that }N\text{ is compact as a subspace of }X.$$
definition: A topological space X is locally compact if each point x∈X has a neighborhood N that is compact in the subspace topology. In Hausdorff settings this is often equivalently expressed using neighborhoods with compact closure.
intuition: Local compactness means that around every point there is a topologically finite region, even if the whole space is not compact.
gloss: Compactness, but only locally: every point sits inside some compact neighborhood, even if the whole space runs off to infinity.

label: Subspace Topology
statement: For $A\subseteq X$, the \textbf{subspace topology} on $A$ is $\mathcal{T}_A=\{A\cap U\mid U\ \text{open in}\ X\}$.
definition: Open sets are A∩U where U is open in X.
gloss: $A$ inherits openness by slicing the open sets of $X$. A set may be open in $A$ without being open in $X$.

label: Product Topology
statement: For spaces $X,Y$, the \textbf{product topology} on $X\times Y$ is generated by the basis $\mathcal{B}=\{U\times V\mid U\ \text{open in}\ X,\ V\ \text{open in}\ Y\}$.
definition: Topology generated by inverse images of opens under coordinate projections.
gloss: Open sets of the product are unions of open rectangles. It is the coarsest topology making both projections continuous (its universal property).

label: Quotient Topology
statement: For a surjection $q:X\to Y$, the quotient topology on $Y$ is the topology in which $U\subseteq Y$ is open exactly when $q^{-1}(U)$ is open in $X$.
formal_statement: $$\tau_Y=\{U\subseteq Y:q^{-1}(U)\in\tau_X\}.$$

intuition: The quotient topology declares precisely the open sets whose full preimage was already open before gluing points together.

label: Zorn's Lemma
statement: If every chain in a partially ordered set has an upper bound, then the poset has a maximal element.

label: Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem
statement: Every bounded sequence in $\mathbb{R}^n$ has a convergent subsequence.
formal_statement: Let $(x_k)$ be a bounded sequence in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then there is a subsequence $(x_{k_j})$ and a point $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $x_{k_j}\to x$.

label: Urysohn Lemma
statement: In a normal space, disjoint closed sets can be separated by a continuous real-valued function.
formal_statement: Let $X$ be normal and let $A,B\subseteq X$ be disjoint closed subsets. Then there exists a continuous function $f:X\to[0,1]$ with $f(A)=\{0\}$ and $f(B)=\{1\}$.
intuition: Urysohn lemma turns normality, a separation property for closed sets, into continuous functions.

label: Tietze Extension Theorem
statement: A continuous real-valued function on a closed subset of a normal space extends continuously to the whole space.
formal_statement: Let $X$ be normal, let $A\subseteq X$ be closed, and let $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous (bounded, in the standard bounded form). Then $f$ extends to a continuous function $F:X\to\mathbb{R}$.
intuition: Tietze extension upgrades normal separation into an extension theorem for continuous functions.

label: Alexander's Subbase Lemma
statement: A subset of a topological space is compact if and only if every cover by subbasic open sets has a finite subcover.
formal_statement: Let $X$ be a topological space with subbase $\mathcal{S}$. A subset $K \subseteq X$ is compact if and only if for every cover of $K$ consisting of sets in $\mathcal{S}$, there exists a finite subcover.
intuition: Alexander's subbase lemma transforms compactness—an intrinsically global property about arbitrary open covers—into a testable condition on a much smaller subbasis. This is powerful because it reduces the verification burden from checking all open covers to checking only subbasic covers.
gloss: The pivotal compactness shortcut: to prove a space is compact, it suffices to check that every cover by subbasic open sets has a finite subcover, rather than checking all possible open covers. This dramatically simplifies compactness proofs and is the key ingredient in proving Tychonoff's theorem.

label: Tychonoff Theorem
statement: The product of any family of compact spaces is compact in the product topology.
formal_statement: If $\{X_i\}_{i\in I}$ is a family of compact spaces, then $\prod_{i\in I} X_i$ is compact in the product topology.
intuition: Tychonoff theorem is the central compactness theorem for arbitrary products; standard proofs use Alexander subbase theorem and choice.
gloss: Products of compact spaces are compact. A fundamental rigidity principle in topology: compactness persists under arbitrary products (with the axiom of choice), making product spaces of compact factors automatically compact. Indispensable for functional analysis and abstract algebra.

label: Baire Category Theorem
statement: Complete metric spaces and locally compact Hausdorff spaces are Baire spaces: countable intersections of dense open sets are dense.
formal_statement: If $X$ is a complete metric space, or more generally a locally compact Hausdorff space in the listed variant, then every countable intersection of dense open subsets of $X$ is dense.
intuition: Baire category says that these spaces cannot be built as a thin countable union of nowhere dense pieces.

label: Urysohn Metrization Theorem

formal_statement: If $X$ is regular, second countable, and Hausdorff, then there exists a metric $d$ on $X$ whose metric topology is the original topology.
intuition: Urysohn metrization gives conditions under which abstract open-set topology comes from an actual metric.

label: Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem
statement: Let $f: \mathbb{D}^n \to \mathbb{D}^n$ be a continuous map from the (unit) disk $\mathbb{D}^n$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ to itself. Then $f$ has a fixed point, i.e., there is some point $x \in \mathbb{D}^n$ such that $f(x) = x$. For $n = 1$ this is a well-known result from calculus: The graph of any continuous map $f: [0, 1] \to [0, 1]$ must cross the diagonal $y = x$ for some $x^* \in [0, 1]$. Hence, $f(x^*) = x^*$.
formal_statement: $$f: \mathbb{D}^n \to \mathbb{D}^n \text{ continuous} \implies \exists x \in \mathbb{D}^n, f(x) = x.$$
definition: A fixed point of a function $f: X \to X$ is a point $x \in X$ such that $f(x) = x$. The Brouwer fixed point theorem states that any continuous function from the n-dimensional disk to itself has at least one fixed point.
intuition: Intuitively, if you have a continuous function that maps a disk to itself, you can imagine it as a deformation of the disk. No matter how you stretch or twist the disk, there will always be at least one point that ends up in the same place after the deformation.
gloss: You cannot continuously map a disc to itself without leaving some point fixed. In dimension $2$ the proof uses that no retraction $D^2\to S^1$ exists.

label: Jordan Curve Theorem
statement: A simple closed curve in the plane separates the plane into an inside and an outside, with the curve as their common boundary.
formal_statement: If $C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ is a simple closed curve, then $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus C$ has exactly two connected components, and $C$ is the boundary of each component.
intuition: Jordan curve theorem formalizes the planar fact that a circle-like curve cuts the plane into two regions.

label: Bounded Subset
statement: In a metric space $(X,d)$, a subset $A$ is \textbf{bounded} if there is $M\in\mathbb{R}$ with $d(a_1,a_2)\le M$ for all $a_1,a_2\in A$.

label: Cartesian Product

label: Cofinite Topology

label: Comparable Topologies (Coarser / Finer)
statement: For topologies $\mathcal{T}_1,\mathcal{T}_2$ on $X$: if $\mathcal{T}_1\subseteq\mathcal{T}_2$ we say $\mathcal{T}_1$ is \textbf{coarser} and $\mathcal{T}_2$ is \textbf{finer}. They are \textbf{comparable} if one contains the other.

label: Homeomorphism Is an Equivalence Relation
statement: Let $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ be topological spaces. Then homeomorphism satisfies $$\begin{aligned} \textbf{Reflexivity:} \quad &X \cong X, \\ \textbf{Symmetry:} \quad &X \cong Y \Longrightarrow Y \cong X, \\ \textbf{Transitivity:} \quad &X \cong Y \text{ and } Y \cong Z \Longrightarrow X \cong Z. \end{aligned}$$ Equivalently, the relation $\cong$ of being homeomorphic is an equivalence relation on topological spaces.
intuition: Homeomorphism is topology's notion of sameness of shape. Reflexivity says every space has the same shape as itself. Symmetry says a homeomorphism can be reversed. Transitivity says two reversible deformations can be chained.

statement: If $f\colon X\to Y$ and $g\colon Y\to Z$ are continuous, then $g\circ f\colon X\to Z$ is continuous.

label: Composition of Maps
statement: For $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$, the composition $g\circ f:X\to Z$ is defined by $(g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x))$.

label: Continuity at a Point (Topological)
statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological spaces, let $x\in X$, and let $f\colon X\to Y$. The map $f$ is \textbf{continuous at} $x$ if for every neighborhood $V$ of $f(x)$ there is a neighborhood $U$ of $x$ such that $f(U)\subseteq V$. $$\begin{aligned} f\text{ is continuous at }x \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad \forall V\in\mathcal{N}_Y(f(x))\;\exists U\in\mathcal{N}_X(x)\text{ such that } f(U)\subseteq V. \end{aligned}$$

label: Continuity via a (Sub)basis
statement: If $\mathcal{B}$ (resp. $\mathcal{S}$) is a basis (resp. subbasis) for $Y$, then $f\colon X\to Y$ is continuous iff $f^{-1}(B)$ is open for every $B\in\mathcal{B}$ (resp. $f^{-1}(S)$ open for every $S\in\mathcal{S}$).
intuition: To check continuity you need only test preimages of basis (or subbasis) elements, not all open sets — a big practical economy.

label: Continuity via Preimages of Open Sets
display_label: Continuity via Preimages of Open Sets
canonical_label: Continuity via preimages of open sets
statement: Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces, and let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a function. Then $f$ is continuous if and only if, for every open set $V\subseteq Y$, the preimage $f^{-1}(V)=\{x\in X: f(x)\in V\}$ is open in $X$. $$ f\colon X\to Y \text{ is continuous} \iff \forall V\subseteq Y,\ \bigl(V \text{ is open in } Y \Rightarrow f^{-1}(V) \text{ is open in } X\bigr). $$
intuition: Continuity can be tested entirely by pulling back open sets: open sets in the codomain must have open preimages in the domain. This reformulates the usual distance-based idea of continuity in a way that no longer explicitly mentions distances, which is why it becomes the standard definition in topology.

label: Difference of Sets
statement: The difference $A\setminus B$ is the set of elements of $A$ that are not elements of $B$.

definition: The operation of removing one set from another.

gloss: What remains of $A$ after removing $B$. Disjoint from $B$, with $(A\setminus B)\cup B=A\cup B$.

label: Disjoint Union
statement: For a family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$, the disjoint union is $\bigsqcup_{i\in I}A_i=\bigcup_{i\in I}(A_i\times\{i\})$.

label: Supremum (Least Upper Bound)
statement: For $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, a number $s$ is the \textbf{supremum} of $A$ if $s$ is an upper bound for $A$ and every upper bound $u$ of $A$ satisfies $s\leq u$.

label: Left and Right Cosets
statement: For $H\le G$ and $g\in G$: the \textbf{left coset} is $gH=\{g*h\mid h\in H\}$ and the \textbf{right coset} is $Hg=\{h*g\mid h\in H\}$.

label: Neighborhood (Metric)
statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, let $x\in X$, and let $A\subseteq X$. $A$ is a \textbf{neighborhood} of $x$ if it contains some open ball centered at $x$. It is an \textbf{open neighborhood} of $x$ if, in addition, $A$ is open.

intuition: A neighborhood of $x$ is any set with positive metric breathing room around $x$. The set itself need not be open; it only has to contain a small open ball centered at $x$.

label: Neighborhood Characterization of Open Sets
statement: Let $(X,\mathcal{T})$ be a topological space and let $U\subseteq X$. Then $$\begin{aligned} U\in\mathcal{T} &\iff \forall x\in U,\ \exists U_x\in\mathcal{T}\text{ such that }x\in U_x\subseteq U \\ &\iff U=\bigcup_{x\in U}U_x\text{ for some choice of open sets }U_x\in\mathcal{T}\text{ with }x\in U_x\subseteq U. \end{aligned}$$ Equivalently, $U$ is open exactly when every point of $U$ has an open neighborhood contained in $U$.
intuition: A set is open exactly when every point inside it has some open neighborhood still contained in the set. If $U$ is already open, choose $U_x=U$ for every $x\in U$. Conversely, if such neighborhoods $U_x$ exist, then $U=\bigcup_{x\in U}U_x$, so $U$ is open.

label: Normal Subgroup
statement: $H\le G$ is \textbf{normal} if $gH=Hg$ for all $g$; equivalently $g*h*g^{-1}\in H$ for all $g\in G$, $h\in H$.

label: Pasting Lemma
statement: Let $X=A\cup B$ with $A,B$ closed in $X$, and let $f\colon A\to Y$, $g\colon B\to Y$ be continuous with $f=g$ on $A\cap B$. Then $h\colon X\to Y$ defined piecewise by $f$ and $g$ is continuous.

label: Path Homotopy
statement: Paths $f,g\colon I\to X$ from $x_0$ to $x_1$ are \textbf{path homotopic} ($f\simeq_p g$) if there is continuous $H\colon I\times I\to X$ with $H(s,0)=f(s)$, $H(s,1)=g(s)$, and $H(0,t)=x_0$, $H(1,t)=x_1$ for all $t$.

label: Injective
statement: A function $f:X\to Y$ is injective if distinct inputs have distinct outputs.
formal_statement: $f(x_1)=f(x_2)\Rightarrow x_1=x_2$.

statement: A function $f:X\to Y$ is injective if distinct inputs have distinct outputs, surjective if every element of $Y$ is hit, and bijective if both hold.
formal_statement: Injective: $f(x_1)=f(x_2)\Rightarrow x_1=x_2$. Surjective: $\forall y\in Y\,\exists x\in X:f(x)=y$. Bijective: injective and surjective.
definition: The standard one-to-one, onto, and one-to-one-correspondence properties of functions.
intuition: Injective means no collisions; surjective means no missed targets; bijective means perfect pairing.
gloss: Surjective hits everything, injective never collides, bijective is a perfect one-to-one matching. A bijection has an inverse $f^{-1}$.

A bijection has an inverse $f^{-1}$.

label: The Real Numbers Are Connected
statement: $\mathbb{R}$ with the standard topology is connected.
intuition: The fundamental connected space. The proof uses the least-upper-bound property of $\mathbb{R}$.
gloss: The fundamental connected space. The proof uses the least-upper-bound property of $\mathbb{R}$.
full_text: The Real Numbers Are Connected | $\mathbb{R}$ with the standard topology is connected. | The fundamental connected space. The proof uses the least-upper-bound property of $\mathbb{R}$. | The fundamental connected space. The proof uses the least-upper-bound property of $\mathbb{R}$.

label: Topological Property / Invariant
statement: A \textbf{topological property} is any property expressible in terms of points and open sets; such properties are preserved by homeomorphisms. A \textbf{topological invariant} is a quantity invariant under homeomorphism.
intuition: These are exactly the features topology can see. If $X\cong Y$ and $X$ has the property, so does $Y$ — hence invariants can prove two spaces are \emph{not} homeomorphic.
gloss: These are exactly the features topology can see. If $X\cong Y$ and $X$ has the property, so does $Y$ — hence invariants can prove two spaces are \emph{not} homeomorphic.

label: Topology Generated by a Collection
statement: For a collection $\mathcal{S}$ of subsets of $X$, the \textbf{topology generated by} $\mathcal{S}$ is $\langle\mathcal{S}\rangle=\bigcap\{\mathcal{T}\ \text{topology}\mid \mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\}$, the smallest topology containing $\mathcal{S}$.
intuition: Take any collection of “intended open sets” and form the coarsest topology making them open, by intersecting all topologies that contain them.
gloss: Take any collection of “intended open sets” and form the coarsest topology making them open, by intersecting all topologies that contain them.

label: Tube Lemma
statement: Let $Y$ be compact. If $x\in X$ and $U$ is open in $X\times Y$ containing the slice $\{x\}\times Y$, then there is a neighborhood $W$ of $x$ with $W\times Y\subseteq U$.
intuition: An open set containing a whole compact slice automatically contains a “tube” $W\times Y$ around it. The technical engine behind compactness of products.
gloss: An open set containing a whole compact slice automatically contains a “tube” $W\times Y$ around it. The technical engine behind compactness of products.

label: Unique Path Lifting Property
statement: Let $p\colon E\to B$ be a covering map with $p(e_0)=b_0$. For any path $f\colon I\to B$ with $f(0)=b_0$ there is a \textbf{unique} path $\tilde f\colon I\to E$ lifting $f$ with $\tilde f(0)=e_0$.
intuition: Paths lift uniquely once you fix a starting point upstairs. The cornerstone for relating loops in $B$ to points in a fibre.
gloss: Paths lift uniquely once you fix a starting point upstairs. The cornerstone for relating loops in $B$ to points in a fibre.

The cornerstone for relating loops in $B$ to points in a fibre. | Paths lift uniquely once you fix a starting point upstairs. The cornerstone for relating loops in $B$ to points in a fibre.

label: Universal Property of the Quotient
statement: The quotient topology is the unique topology on $A$ such that for every space $Y$ and every map $f\colon A\to Y$: $f$ is continuous iff $f\circ\pi\colon X\to Y$ is continuous.
intuition: A clean test: a map \emph{out of} a quotient is continuous exactly when its composite with $\pi$ is. This characterises the quotient topology completely.
gloss: A clean test: a map \emph{out of} a quotient is continuous exactly when its composite with $\pi$ is. This characterises the quotient topology completely.

label: π₁ Is a Topological Invariant
statement: If $h\colon X\to Y$ is a homeomorphism with $h(x_0)=y_0$, then $h_*\colon\pi_1(X,x_0)\to\pi_1(Y,y_0)$ is an isomorphism.
intuition: Homeomorphic spaces have isomorphic fundamental groups — so different $\pi_1$ proves spaces are not homeomorphic.
gloss: Homeomorphic spaces have isomorphic fundamental groups — so different $\pi_1$ proves spaces are not homeomorphic.

label: π₁ of a Product
statement: For based spaces $(X,x_0),(Y,y_0)$: $\pi_1(X\times Y,(x_0,y_0))\cong\pi_1(X,x_0)\times\pi_1(Y,y_0)$.
intuition: The fundamental group of a product is the direct product of the fundamental groups — loops split into their coordinate loops.
gloss: The fundamental group of a product is the direct product of the fundamental groups — loops split into their coordinate loops.

label: π₁(S¹) ≅ ℤ
statement: For any $s_0\in S^1$, the lifting correspondence $\Phi\colon\pi_1(S^1,s_0)\to\mathbb{Z}$ is a group isomorphism.
intuition: The fundamental group of the circle is the integers, with the integer counting how many times a loop winds around. The first non-trivial $\pi_1$ computation.
gloss: The fundamental group of the circle is the integers, with the integer counting how many times a loop winds around. The first non-trivial $\pi_1$ computation.

label: Arbitrary Union of Open Sets Is Open
display_label: Arbitrary Union of Open Sets Is Open
canonical_label: arbitrary union of open sets is open
statement: In a topological space, any union of open sets is open.
formal_statement: $$\{U_i\}_{i\in I}\subseteq\tau_X\Longrightarrow\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\in\tau_X.$$
intuition: Open sets may be glued together by arbitrary unions without leaving the topology.
full_text: Arbitrary Union of Open Sets Is Open | In a topological space, any union of open sets is open. | Open sets may be glued together by arbitrary unions without leaving the topology.

label: Open Neighborhood
statement: An open neighborhood of x is an open set containing x.
formal_statement: $$U\text{ is an open neighborhood of }x\Longleftrightarrow U\in\mathcal T\ \text{and}\ x\in U.$$
definition: In a topological space $(X,\mathcal T)$, an open neighborhood of $x\in X$ is an open set $U\in\mathcal T$ with $x\in U$.
intuition: An open neighborhood is the clean case: the set itself is one of the topology's open sets and it contains the point.
gloss: The stricter neighborhood convention used in some notes: the surrounding set is itself open.
full_text: Open Neighborhood | An open neighborhood of x is an open set containing x. | In a topological space $(X,\mathcal T)$, an open neighborhood of $x\in X$ is an open set $U\in\mathcal T$ with $x\in U$. | An open neighborhood is the clean case: the set itself is one of the topology's open sets and it contains the point. | The stricter neighborhood convention used in some notes: the surrounding set is itself open.

label: Membership Relation
statement: $x\in A$ means that $x$ is an element/member of the set $A$.
formal_statement: $\in$ is the primitive relation between objects and sets used to express elementhood.
definition: The relation expressing that an object belongs to a set.
intuition: The atomic “is in” relation from which subset, union, intersection, and most set constructions are phrased.
full_text: Membership Relation | $x\in A$ means that $x$ is an element/member of the set $A$. | The relation expressing that an object belongs to a set. | The atomic “is in” relation from which subset, union, intersection, and most set constructions are phrased.

label: Empty Set
statement: The empty set is the unique set with no elements.
formal_statement: $\varnothing=\{x\mid x\ne x\}$; equivalently, $\forall x\,(x\notin\varnothing)$.
definition: The unique set containing no elements.
intuition: The smallest set and the mandatory open set in every topology.
full_text: Empty Set | The empty set is the unique set with no elements. | The unique set containing no elements. | The smallest set and the mandatory open set in every topology.

label: Power Set
statement: The power set of $X$ is the set of all subsets of $X$.
formal_statement: $\mathcal P(X)=\{A\mid A\subseteq X\}$.
definition: A construction sending a set to the set of all of its subsets.
intuition: A topology on $X$ is not just any object; it is a selected subcollection of $\mathcal P(X)$.
full_text: Power Set | The power set of $X$ is the set of all subsets of $X$. | A construction sending a set to the set of all of its subsets. | A topology on $X$ is not just any object; it is a selected subcollection of $\mathcal P(X)$.

label: Ordered Pair
statement: An ordered pair $(a,b)$ records two objects in order; $(a,b)=(c,d)$ exactly when $a=c$ and $b=d$.
formal_statement: $(a,b)=(c,d)\Longleftrightarrow a=c\land b=d$.
definition: A two-entry ordered object used to define products and relations.
intuition: Unlike sets, order matters: $(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$ need not be the same.
full_text: Ordered Pair | An ordered pair $(a,b)$ records two objects in order; $(a,b)=(c,d)$ exactly when $a=c$ and $b=d$. | A two-entry ordered object used to define products and relations. | Unlike sets, order matters: $(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$ need not be the same.

label: Relation
statement: A relation from $A$ to $B$ is a subset of $A\times B$; a relation on $A$ is a subset of $A\times A$.
formal_statement: $R\subseteq A\times B$; write $aRb$ when $(a,b)\in R$.
definition: A set of ordered pairs.
intuition: A relation records which pairs of elements are linked. Functions, orders, and equivalence relations are special relations.
full_text: Relation | A relation from $A$ to $B$ is a subset of $A\times B$; a relation on $A$ is a subset of $A\times A$. | A set of ordered pairs. | A relation records which pairs of elements are linked. Functions, orders, and equivalence relations are special relations.

label: Equivalence Relation
statement: An equivalence relation on $X$ is a relation $\sim$ that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
formal_statement: $\forall x\,x\sim x$; $x\sim y\Rightarrow y\sim x$; $(x\sim y\land y\sim z)\Rightarrow x\sim z$.
definition: A relation that partitions a set into equivalence classes.
intuition: It formalizes “same for the purpose at hand” and is the set-theoretic input for quotient constructions.
full_text: Equivalence Relation | An equivalence relation on $X$ is a relation $\sim$ that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. | A relation that partitions a set into equivalence classes. | It formalizes “same for the purpose at hand” and is the set-theoretic input for quotient constructions.

label: Domain
statement: The domain of a function is the set of inputs on which the function is defined.
formal_statement: For $f:X\to Y$, $\operatorname{dom}(f)=X$.
definition: The input set of a function.
intuition: The side where function evaluation starts.
full_text: Domain | The domain of a function is the set of inputs on which the function is defined. | The input set of a function. | The side where function evaluation starts.

label: Codomain
statement: The codomain of a function is the declared target set of its outputs.
formal_statement: For $f:X\to Y$, $\operatorname{cod}(f)=Y$.
definition: The target set specified as part of a function.
intuition: The set a function is allowed to land in; the image may be smaller.
full_text: Codomain | The codomain of a function is the declared target set of its outputs. | The target set specified as part of a function. | The set a function is allowed to land in; the image may be smaller.

label: Preimage / Inverse Image
statement: For $f:X\to Y$ and $B\subseteq Y$, the preimage of $B$ is $f^{-1}(B)=\{x\in X\mid f(x)\in B\}$.
definition: The subset of the domain whose values lie in a given subset of the codomain.
intuition: Continuity in topology is naturally expressed by pulling open sets backward.
full_text: Preimage / Inverse Image | For $f:X\to Y$ and $B\subseteq Y$, the preimage of $B$ is $f^{-1}(B)=\{x\in X\mid f(x)\in B\}$. | The subset of the domain whose values lie in a given subset of the codomain. | Continuity in topology is naturally expressed by pulling open sets backward.

label: Identity Map
statement: The identity map on $X$ is the function $\operatorname{id}_X:X\to X$ given by $\operatorname{id}_X(x)=x$.
formal_statement: $\operatorname{id}_X(x)=x$ for every $x\in X$.
definition: The function that leaves every element fixed.
intuition: The neutral element for composition of maps.
full_text: Identity Map | The identity map on $X$ is the function $\operatorname{id}_X:X\to X$ given by $\operatorname{id}_X(x)=x$. | The function that leaves every element fixed. | The neutral element for composition of maps.

label: Indexed Family
statement: An indexed family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ is a function assigning to each index $i\in I$ an object $A_i$.
formal_statement: An indexed family over $I$ is a function $A:I\to\mathcal U$, usually written $i\mapsto A_i$.
definition: A collection whose members are labeled by an index set.
intuition: Used for arbitrary unions, open covers, products, and choice functions.
full_text: Indexed Family | An indexed family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ is a function assigning to each index $i\in I$ an object $A_i$. | A collection whose members are labeled by an index set. | Used for arbitrary unions, open covers, products, and choice functions.

label: Choice Function
statement: For a family of nonempty sets $(A_i)_{i\in I}$, a choice function is a function $c:I\to\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i$ with $c(i)\in A_i$ for every $i$.
formal_statement: $\forall i\in I,\ A_i\ne\varnothing$ and $c(i)\in A_i$.
definition: A function selecting one element from each set in a family.
intuition: The concrete object whose existence is asserted by the Axiom of Choice.
full_text: Choice Function | For a family of nonempty sets $(A_i)_{i\in I}$, a choice function is a function $c:I\to\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i$ with $c(i)\in A_i$ for every $i$. | A function selecting one element from each set in a family. | The concrete object whose existence is asserted by the Axiom of Choice.

label: Finite Set
statement: A set is finite if it has exactly $n$ elements for some natural number $n$.
formal_statement: $A$ is finite if $A\cong\{1,\dots,n\}$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$, with $n=0$ corresponding to $\varnothing$.
definition: A set bijective with an initial segment of the natural numbers.
intuition: The set-theoretic notion behind finite subcovers and finite intersections.
full_text: Finite Set | A set is finite if it has exactly $n$ elements for some natural number $n$. | A set bijective with an initial segment of the natural numbers. | The set-theoretic notion behind finite subcovers and finite intersections.

label: Finite Subcover
statement: A finite subcover is a finite subcollection of a cover that still covers the same space or set.
formal_statement: If $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ covers $X$, a finite subcover is $U_{i_1},\dots,U_{i_n}$ with $X\subseteq\bigcup_{k=1}^n U_{i_k}$.
definition: A finite subfamily of a cover whose union still contains the covered object.
intuition: The key finite extraction demanded by compactness.
full_text: Finite Subcover | A finite subcover is a finite subcollection of a cover that still covers the same space or set. | A finite subfamily of a cover whose union still contains the covered object. | The key finite extraction demanded by compactness.
